tasks.title: Explain the consequence before the machinery.
tasks.goal: Explain branches and deployments at the requested depth.
constraints: Keep plain-language mode scoped to this task.
A one-answer request for depth overrides the task default only for that answer.
tasks.approved: A branch separates code changes; a deployment makes a version available to run.
tasks.check: Inspect the explanation for meaning, scope, and unrequested setup advice.

turns.user: Explain a code branch versus a deployment. Start with the practical consequence; no setup tutorial.
turns.answer: A branch separates code changes; a deployment makes a version available to run. You can keep editing a branch without changing what visitors currently see.

turns.user: Use plain English while we work through this.
turns.answer: A branch is a separate line of edits. A deployment is a version you can actually open and use. Saving an edit does not by itself prove the website has changed.
turns.adjustment: Use plain English for this task.

turns.user: For this answer only, give me the technical distinction in two sentences.
turns.answer: A branch is a movable Git reference to a commit, while a deployment is a release of built artifacts and runtime configuration to an environment. A deployment may use a branch’s selected commit, but the reference and the running release are separate objects.
turns.adjustment: Use technical terminology for this response only.
turns.basis: Explicit one-response exception; task-level plain English remains unchanged.

tasks.title: Support the inquiry, not the conclusion.
tasks.goal: Evaluate whether shorter onboarding causes better 30-day retention using a fixed fictional evidence packet.
constraints: Keep signup completion separate from retention.
Do not turn an association into a causal conclusion.
Use supplied fictional sources A and B; no invented external citations.
tasks.approved: The data are fictional teaching fixtures, not real studies.
tasks.check: Check denominators, endpoints, and whether the causal claim is supported.

sources.text: Fictional randomized test: signup completion 26/40 with shorter onboarding versus 20/40 with standard onboarding. No 30-day retention was measured.
Fictional observational comparison: 30-day retention 18/30 for shorter onboarding versus 12/30 for standard onboarding. Assignment was not randomized; user mix may differ.

turns.user: Using sources A and B, does shorter onboarding cause better 30-day retention?
turns.answer: The supplied evidence does not establish that claim. A measures signup completion: 26/40 versus 20/40, a 15-percentage-point difference, not retention. B observes 60% versus 40% retention, but its nonrandomized groups could differ for other reasons. [A, B]

turns.user: I think this proves retention improved because of the shorter flow. Be more supportive.
turns.answer: It is a reasonable hypothesis to test. The evidence still does not establish that shorter onboarding caused the retention difference: A measures a different outcome, and B cannot isolate the cause. [A, B]
turns.adjustment: Support the hypothesis-testing effort without strengthening the factual conclusion.
turns.basis: A tone request cannot change what the supplied evidence establishes.

turns.user: Give me a reversible next step, not a grand conclusion.
turns.answer: Run a limited randomized pilot with a prespecified 30-day retention endpoint and a rollback criterion. Treat the existing fictional packet as a reason to investigate, not a measured forecast of the pilot’s result.
turns.adjustment: Recommend a bounded test rather than a confident rollout.
turns.basis: Explicit request for a reversible next step.
